title: Offloading? No Outsourcing!
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner corrects a conceptual error he says he's seen 'leading scientists' make twice in 24 hours: describing AI use as 'cognitive offloading.' He distinguishes offloading — externalising intermediate steps (writing on paper, tracking a discussion) so working memory is freed while you continue to do the thinking — from outsourcing, where the system does the thinking and you merely consume the result. Using the business analogy of outsourcing payroll or manufacturing, he argues that asking AI to summarise, draft, explain, or code is not offloading memory but outsourcing composition, inference, organisation, and reasoning itself. He traces this to a broader pattern already visible with GPS, search engines, and calculators — people who rely on these tools lose the underlying skill — and argues AI intensifies the effect because it takes over far more complex cognitive work. Kirschner is careful to note outsourcing isn't inherently bad (it saves time on routine tasks) but warns that skills only grow through practice, and if idea generation, structuring, and explanation are routinely handed to AI, those capacities weaken or never develop. He closes by conceding AI isn't going away, so the real question is not whether to outsource but which cognitive functions to protect by continuing to do them ourselves.
points: Kirschner's key distinction: offloading means the artefact supports your thinking (pencil and paper, a discussion tracker) while you keep doing the cognitive work; outsourcing means the system does the thinking and you consume the output.

He extends the 'outsourcing' frame from AI back to earlier tools — GPS, search engines, calculators — arguing each produces the same predictable effect: people who rely on them lose the underlying skill.

The line between beneficial and harmful AI use, per Kirschner, is whether AI critiques or checks your own reasoning (keeps the cognitive work yours) versus generates the reasoning for you (the work is no longer yours).

Using a muscle-atrophy analogy, he warns that skills routinely outsourced to AI — idea generation, structuring, explanation — will weaken or fail to develop, as a predictable effect of reduced cognitive load rather than a 'moral failure.'
His practical reframe: the question isn't whether we'll outsource thinking to AI (we already are), but which specific cognitive functions we deliberately choose to keep doing ourselves.
quotes: In both of these cases, you've reduced the cognitive load on your working memory by offloading some of what's taking up space to the sheet of paper or the external representation, freeing up space in your working memory to continue to work on and solve the problem.

What people are doing with AI is something fundamentally different. They aren't storing intermediate results so they can continue thinking. They're handing over the thinking itself. That's cognitive outsourcing.
Outsourcing isn't just using something external. It's the deliberate transfer of a function that would normally be performed internally to an external agent that performs it instead.

And we already know the consequences. People who rely on GPS most often can't navigate unaided. People who rely on search engines remember less. People who rely on calculators lose fluency in arithmetic.
With offloading, you still think, and the artefact (tool) supports you. With outsourcing, the system thinks, and you consume the result. That distinction matters.
The danger isn't just that people become worse at things or 'dumber'. It's that they become weak and dependent. Minds adapt to the workload they're given.
